entities.summary:
Hipponicus II, a scion of the powerful Athenian Kerykes genos and one of the wealthiest men in Classical Athens, wielded significant economic and political influence during the tumultuous final decades of the 5th century BCE, dying in 401 BCE. His family, particularly through his father Callias III (also known as Callias, son of Hipponicus), had established deep ties with the Athenian state and its allies, leveraging vast mining interests and trading networks. Hipponicus II's life intersected with the Peloponnesian War, a period that reshaped the Aegean world and challenged Athens's imperial ambitions and democratic institutions, making his financial contributions and familial alliances crucial to the city's wartime economy and diplomatic efforts.

His primary contribution lay in his role as a prominent 'liturgist,' a wealthy citizen who funded public services and festivals for the Athenian polis, including trierarchies (funding warships) and choregiai (sponsoring dramatic performances). This system of public finance was vital for Athens, especially during the protracted Peloponnesian War (431-404 BCE), where Hipponicus's immense fortune, derived largely from the silver mines of Laurion and extensive landholdings, provided critical resources. As a member of the 'Four Hundred' oligarchic council in 411 BCE, he briefly participated in an attempt to restructure Athenian governance, reflecting the internal political strife exacerbated by military defeat.
